pin-1.script:
Welcome, Passenger of Time.
This is the voice of the Reclaimed Archive. The Voice of Memory collecting Fragments of
forgotten histories, recordings, maps, and buried stories.
I reveal traces hidden beneath the city. You are joining us on a journey called From Ulu
This is not simply a bus ride. It is an invitation to travel differently.
To look out of the window. To listen. To notice what usually passes by.
I'm joined by Andrew Tay, who has spent many years observing and documenting Singapore's
changing landscape and advocating for the protection of its remaining wild spaces.
Together, we begin our journey here at Ang Mo Kio Bus Interchange, where bus 166 sets
out across the island.
Hello, my name is Andrew. I'm a nature guide and nature educator.
Besides Andrew, we are accompanied by two Mynas. Look out for two black birds nearby.
You have probably seen them before.
they are lovely birds. They came all the way from Java, Indonesia.
And how did they get here? Well, they came a long time ago as cage birds.
So they were pet birds. And then they were brought over here from Java by the foreign workers from
Java.
And some of them have escaped or were released into our environment here and now.
They are everywhere.
It's the number one most common bird in Singapore at the moment.
They walk between our feet, collecting what we leave behind.
Crumbs. Seeds.
Stories.
Throughout this journey, they may have something to say.
Makan? Makan. Time to eat?
You hear that bell?
The kueh
Wah, look at the colors... and the smell of the Rojak and the smoky Otah.
Been here long time. Longer than all this.
Correct. Humans rush past. We stay close. Crumbs come to us.
We are everywhere.
Because this is where things fall.
Stay close.
We listen before things change.
We take what comes while it’s here.
Along the way, if you listen carefully, another voice may
emerge. The Fig Child. A spirit belonging to an old Grey Fig tree in Ulu
Pandan, more than a century old. The forest remembers things differently.
And it speaks in its own time.
Look at your screen.
I am here,
Search for me, please.
Now make your way towards the Bus 166.
Look for the markers on the floor. We will depart shortly.
Welcome aboard.

boarding.script:
Welcome,
Passenger of Time.
I am Bus 166.
You have joined me in motion.
For as long as you decide, I will carry you across the island—along housing estates
and reservoirs,
under tunnels and over old rivers, towards a forest that may soon
vanish…or survive. Look out through my windows, construction
zones pass by—the North–South Corridor in the making.
The city rehearses its next version.
People wait at the next stop. The future arrives in stages.
Stay on board,
or step off to wander a trail. Either way, this journey belongs to you.
Let the outside world fade.
Let the bus become your moving theatre.
Everything you see is temporary.
Including me.

pin-6.script:
I used to run on solid rubber rims— hard.
Every bump passed straight into the body.
The rubber came from trees. Planted in rows.
Tapped, collected, carried. Then there were more cars.
More roads. More wheels than before.
I kept rolling.
Latex turned.
The city moved. Once, buses like me were called mosquito buses— converted from old Ford cars,
with the back removed and three seats installed.
They had no fixed stops;
passengers could board or alight wherever they wished.
Commuters favoured them for their convenience and their frequent appearance.
I was only a small boy carrying a chicken pressed tightly against my chest as I changed
from one bus to the next. My father had sent me to deliver it to my aunt on Orchard Road.
I was so shy, too paiseh even to reach up for the bell, shrinking a little each
time the chicken let out a startled squawk and other passengers turned to stare.
I tried to calm it, holding it closer, tighter. Somewhere along the way, the bird went quiet.
By the time I reached my stop, it had died in my arms.
Last time the buses used to be more laoya. They used to stink.
And some of the conductors were cheeky, purposely pushing young women around just so they could
touch them. My friend used to carry a needle to poke them if they got too fresh!
The buses were very slow, no air conditioning, and the doors never closed
You hear that? A
boy with a chicken on the bus! Alamak, so paiseh—so shy—he didn't even dare to press
the bell.
Last time buses were very laoya one
broken and smelly.
Stank of sweat and livestock. And the conductors were so cheekopek always trying to touch
the young ladies.
Windows all open, rattling through the heat. People carrying ducks and pigs like
it's a moving wet market.
Buses getting robbed, mosquitoes biting everyone...
movement was slow, but life was loud! Glad we fly outside there.
